rv.q: Suddenly, this story seems tailor-made for the stage.

This may not be as terrifying as the massive Moby Dick-like mammal in the movie but, like everything else in this production, it shows how the fable of the puppet who wants to be human has been delightfully reanimated.
Jamie Harrison, who worked with Tiffany on Harry Potter and the Cursed Child, creates illusions that are effective and plentiful.

When Pinocchio's nose extends to the length of a broomstick or a troupe of marionettes suspended by ribbons accompanies him as he dances, it's impossible not to be impressed by the ingenious effects. Yet spectacle prevails over heart and soul. It's as if the show's formidable technical demands have compromised everything else.
It's reassuring, in this age of Xboxes, Imaxes and metaverses, to discover that children can still let out a scream of satisfaction when they see a modest shower of glitter drift down like snow.

The production by John Tiffany (Harry Potter and the Cursed Child) is fairly lavish but it is beautifully proportioned so that we're always reminded that, at the heart of the piece, there's a simple fervent story about a wooden puppet's quest to be a real boy...
The way that Tiffany and his team have dealt with Pinocchio’s deep-sea journey is spectacular and magical.
The argument is pretty persuasive, but that doesn’t mean the result fully satisfies on its own terms.
Actually, I thought it was horrid.
This is really stirring stuff and should appeal to young and old alike, building to a happy ending, which also confirms any doubts about whether or not Pinocchio is a morality tale.
This is a production that soars above the rest.

Martin Lowe's folk score is pleasant but unlikely to stick; the numbers you'll come out humming are the movie classics like "I've Got No Strings", "Give a Little Whistle" and "When You Wish Upon a Star"
For all its staggering stagecraft, this "Pinocchio" is, for the moment, missing real soul.
But rather like Pinocchio himself, it just stubbornly fails to come to full, breathing life.
All in all, it's a production to admire rather than fall in love with.
The multilayered storytelling risks becoming muddled, yet its ingenuity is rewarding.

This surprisingly dark message for a show aimed at children (although equally enjoyable for adults) is married, in John Tiffany’s ingenious production, to some remarkable special effects, ranging from a flamelike Blue Fairy to a spectacular sequence in the belly of a whale.
John Tiffany, director of Harry The Cursed Child, brings all his gifts of illusion to Dennis Kelly's script.

cn.t: A visually striking but emotionally hollow adaptation that dazzles with stagecraft and puppetry yet struggles to find its soul. Critics praise the spectacle and darker tone but note a lifeless quality and uneven pacing.
